slides.page_title: What TCP Is and Why It Exists

items: Connection-oriented, reliable, ordered byte-stream transport (RFC 793, updated 9293)
Runs over IP: unreliable, best-effort datagrams
IP gives loss, duplication, reordering, corruption, variable delay
TCP's whole job is hiding those five from the app
Two write() of 100 B may arrive as one read() of 200
Or as four reads of 50. TCP never frames for you
Apps frame themselves: length prefix or delimiter

lines: body = recv_exact(n)   # loop until n bytes
# one recv() can return a partial body

items: The 4-tuple: src IP, src port, dst IP, dst port
Two connections may share 3 fields, never all 4
Full-duplex: each direction has its own seq space, window, close
Flow control: fast sender vs slow receiver's buffer
Congestion control: senders vs routers in the middle
Effective send window = min(rwnd, cwnd) — smaller one is your bottleneck

slides.page_title: What TCP Is and Why It Exists (cont.)

items: Layer 4 of the OSI model
Cost of guarantees: head-of-line blocking
Plus 1 RTT setup and per-connection kernel state
Exactly why QUIC and UDP protocols exist

rows: Byte offset of first data byte

items: 20 bytes min, 60 max; Data Offset counts 32-bit words
Offset 5 = 20 bytes, 15 = 60 bytes
Ack field valid only when the ACK flag is set
Pseudo-header (src IP, dst IP, proto, len) catches IP address corruption
SYN sync seq, ACK ack valid, FIN no more data
RST abort, PSH deliver now, URG urgent pointer
ECE / CWR / NS carry ECN signalling

blocks.title: Skip URG
blocks.text: Urgent Pointer means different things in BSD vs the RFC. Ambiguous across stacks — never build on it.

items: MSS, Window Scale (shift 0-14), SACK-Permitted, Timestamps (TSval/TSecr)
NOP / EOL pad options to 4-byte alignment
Negotiated in SYN + SYN-ACK, then fixed for the connection's life

blocks.title: Middlebox Tax
blocks.text: A box that strips Window Scale from the SYN leaves you at a 64 KB window forever. There is no renegotiation.

items: Ethernet: 1500 MTU − 20 IP − 20 TCP = 1460 bytes
MSS never counts the headers
SYN and FIN each consume one sequence number with no data
That is why the ack is ISN+1
Client ESTABLISHED on step 2 arriving; server on step 3
Both sides must sync seq and confirm the other's ISN arrived
Two-way cannot reject a delayed duplicate SYN from an old connection
Cost: 1 full RTT before byte one
Add 1 RTT for TLS 1.3, 2 for TLS 1.2
RFC 6528: hash(4-tuple + secret) plus a clock
Defends against off-path guessing and blind injection
Predictable ISNs were the classic Mitnick-era hole
SYN queue: half-open, SYN_RECV, sized by tcp_max_syn_backlog
Accept queue: established, waiting on accept()
Accept queue size = min(backlog arg, somaxconn)
Spoofed SYNs never send step 3; SYN queue exhausts
tcp_syncookies=1: state encoded into ISN_s, no queue entry
Options that don't fit the cookie are lost — overload valve, not steady state
TFO (RFC 7413): data in the SYN via server cookie, saves 1 RTT
TFO deployment limited by middlebox breakage and replay concerns
Simultaneous open: both go SYN_SENT→SYN_RECV→ESTAB, legal and unambiguous
No listener → RST → instant 'Connection refused'
Firewall drop → SYN retries 1s, 2s, 4s… ~130 s then ETIMEDOUT
seq=1000 carrying 500 B covers bytes 1000-1499; next starts 1500
ACK is cumulative: 'I have everything below this byte'
ACK 1500 covers all bytes ≤1499, whatever carried them
32-bit space wraps at ~4.29 GB
At 10 Gbps that is ~3.4 s → Timestamps + PAWS mandatory (RFC 7323)
All comparisons are modulo-2^32, never a plain <
Tools show relative seq starting at 1; the raw ISN is hidden
Out-of-order segment → receiver instantly repeats the same cumulative ACK
3 dupACKs is the fast-retransmit loss signal
Delayed ACK waits ≤500 ms (Linux ~40 ms) to piggyback on data
RFC 1122: must ACK at least every 2nd segment
SACK (RFC 2018) carries 3-4 blocks of received non-contiguous ranges
Sender retransmits only the true holes, not everything after the gap
D-SACK (RFC 2883) reports a duplicate arrival
Sender learns it retransmitted needlessly and undoes the cwnd cut

lines: next ACK jumps to 5000   # hole filled

items: An ACK for a retransmit may answer either copy
So RTT samples from retransmitted segments are discarded
Timestamps resolve it exactly and restore the sample

blocks.text: 7. RST vs FIN In Seq Space

items: FIN: orderly close, consumes one sequence number
RST: abort, no delivery guarantee, buffered data discarded
RFC: initial RTO 1 s, minimum 1 s
Linux: TCP_RTO_MIN 200 ms, max 120 s
Every consecutive RTO doubles: 200→400→800→1600 ms
Repeated timeouts are a latency catastrophe
RFC 5681: on the 3rd dupACK resend the hole, skip the RTO wait
Fast recovery halves cwnd instead of collapsing to 1 MSS
Inflate window +1 MSS per extra dupACK to keep the pipe moving
RFC 8985, Linux default: time-based loss detection
Uses per-segment transmit times, not dupACK counting
TLP (Tail Loss Probe) recovers lost tail segments without a full RTO
Last segments lost → no later segments → no dupACKs
Recovery falls back to the RTO timer
TLP exists specifically for this case
Reordering can trigger fast retransmit when nothing was lost
D-SACK plus F-RTO detect it and undo the cwnd reduction
Without SACK a single hole forces go-back-N-like resending
Receiver buffers out-of-order data but cannot deliver it
One lost packet stalls the whole stream
Including unrelated HTTP/2 streams on the same connection

slides.page_title: Modern Recovery and the Sliding Window

items: Receiver advertises free buffer so the sender never overruns it
About the endpoint, not the network
Usable window = rwnd − bytes sent but unacked; at 0 the sender stops
RFC 7323: advertised window × 2^shift, shift 0-14, ~1 GB max
Negotiated only in the SYN — both sides must offer it
BDP = bandwidth × RTT
1 Gbps at 100 ms RTT needs ~12.5 MB in flight vs a 64 KB ceiling
win=0 means the receive buffer is full, usually a stalled app
Sender freezes and starts zero-window probes (persist timer)
Probe is a 1-byte segment eliciting a window update
A pure window-update ACK is never retransmitted — without probes, deadlock
App reads a few bytes → receiver advertises tiny windows
Sender ships 40 bytes of header for 1 byte of data
Clark's fix: withhold the update until a full MSS or half the buffer
Nagle fixes the sender half of the same disease
Nagle: at most one small unacked segment outstanding
Buffers small writes until the ACK lands or an MSS accumulates
Nagle + delayed ACK = the classic 40 ms stall — each waits for the other
Request/response protocols must set TCP_NODELAY

lines: /* TCP_CORK: hold until MSS or 200 ms */

blocks.title: Leave Autotuning On
blocks.text: Linux sizes buffers between tcp_rmem / tcp_wmem bounds. Setting SO_RCVBUF or SO_SNDBUF by hand disables autotuning — usually a downgrade.

items: 1986 NSFNET congestion collapse: 32 kbps → 40 bps, ~1000× drop
Retransmissions of already-queued packets fed the fire
Van Jacobson's 1988 algorithms are the fix we still run
cwnd is sender-side state with no wire representation
The receiver never sees it; only rwnd is advertised
Send limit = min(cwnd, rwnd), measured as SND.NXT − SND.UNA
cwnd starts at IW = 10 MSS (RFC 6928; was 1-4)
cwnd += 1 MSS per ACK → doubles every RTT
Exponential growth, not slow

lines: slow start:  cwnd += MSS        per ACK
# the second is ~ +1 MSS per RTT, linear

items: Additive Increase +1 MSS/RTT, Multiplicative Decrease ×0.5 on loss
AIMD provably converges to fairness at a shared bottleneck
AIAD and MIMD do not converge
Classic TCP reads packet loss as 'router queue full'
On wireless, loss is corruption — the assumption breaks
Result: needless throughput collapse on a healthy link
cwnd climbs linearly, halves on loss, climbs again
One AIMD flow on a full-BDP buffer averages ~75% utilisation
Bufferbloat: oversized unmanaged buffers fill before loss is seen
Seconds of queuing delay; fix with AQM (CoDel, fq_codel) or delay-based CC
RFC 3168: router marks the IP CE bit instead of dropping
Receiver echoes ECE, sender responds CWR and cuts cwnd — zero loss
Idle connection's cwnd is stale; Linux decays it (tcp_slow_start_after_idle)
That is why the first burst on a reused keep-alive connection is slow
Tahoe (1988): slow start, avoidance, fast retransmit; any loss → cwnd 1
Reno: adds fast recovery, cwnd halves; poor with multiple losses
NewReno (RFC 6582): partial ACKs keep it in recovery until all holes fill
NewReno is the reference baseline everything is measured against
CUBIC (RFC 8312, Linux default since 2.6.19): window is a cubic function of time
Independent of RTT — aggressive far from W_max, cautious near it
RTT-fair and scales to high BDP
BBR models the path: estimates delivery rate + min RTT, paces at bottleneck rate
BBR keeps a small queue — great on lossy or bufferbloated paths
BBRv1 could be unfair to CUBIC and build standing queues in shallow buffers
BBRv2/v3 add ECN response and loss awareness
Vegas is delay-based: infers congestion from rising RTT before loss
Low latency, but backs off while loss-based flows do not — it starves
DCTCP: fine-grained ECN marking scales the cut to the marked fraction
Holds queues to a few packets; needs switch support, data center only
Sending a whole cwnd as a burst spikes queues and causes loss
fq qdisc plus internal pacing smooths transmission
BBR requires pacing to function at all

blocks.title: Choosing
blocks.text: Keep CUBIC for typical server traffic. Consider BBR for high-RTT, lossy or video paths. Measure with real traffic — CC interacts with qdisc, AQM and receiver buffers.

items: Four segments because each direction closes independently: FIN, ACK, FIN, ACK
Active closer: ESTAB → FIN_WAIT_1 → FIN_WAIT_2 → TIME_WAIT → CLOSED after 2×MSL
Passive closer: ESTAB → CLOSE_WAIT → LAST_ACK → CLOSED on the final ACK
shutdown(fd, SHUT_WR) sends FIN but keeps reading
Peer sees EOF on read yet can still send
Basis of protocols that stream a request then read the response
CLOSE_WAIT is always an app bug: leaked fd or a missing close in an error path
Linux reaps orphaned FIN_WAIT_2 after tcp_fin_timeout, default 60 s
RST on data to a closed socket, close() with SO_LINGER 0, or no listener
Unsent buffered data is discarded; peer sees ECONNRESET
Simultaneous close: both FIN at once, both go CLOSING → TIME_WAIT

blocks.title: Who Pays
blocks.text: Nothing acknowledges the final ACK — that asymmetry is why TIME_WAIT exists on the active closer. Whoever closes first pays. Under churn, architect so the client closes.

items: After the final ACK, the socket holds the 4-tuple for 2×MSL
Linux hardcodes 60 s (TCP_TIMEWAIT_LEN) — no sysctl for it
RFC 793 sets MSL at 2 min, so 2×MSL = 4 min in theory
BSD and Linux use shorter practical values
Reason 1: if the final ACK is lost, the peer retransmits its FIN
A TIME_WAIT socket re-ACKs it; a closed one sends RST and breaks a clean close
Reason 2: delayed duplicates of this incarnation must die first
Otherwise stale data is injected into a new connection on the same 4-tuple

blocks.title: Not A Leak
blocks.text: TIME_WAIT is not a bug. It is the protocol working. Thousands on a busy proxy is normal.

caption.text: Most "TCP problems" are not TCP's fault — they're an app that never called close(), a middlebox that stripped Window Scale, or a keepalive timer set above your load balancer's. This is the whole protocol on 10 pages: handshake and ISN randomisation, cumulative ACKs and SACK, RTO math, CUBIC vs BBR, the four-way close, and why TIME_WAIT is the protocol working correctly. Save it for the next incident where the graph flatlines at exactly 64 KB / RTT.
